narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the law school decided to reject your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons the model expected you to struggle. Being in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. These early and sustained academic rankings signaled to the model that you would likely find the bar exam especially difficult.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most important factor. While this score is only slightly below the average of 37 for accepted students, it still nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this modest positive influence was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving in these areas would significantly improve your chances in future applications. (198 words)
